strengths: The paper explores an interesting and timely problem at the intersection of algorithmic predictions and combinatorial optimization, specifically investigating how multicalibration can be used to improve downstream decision-making.
The manuscript is clearly structured, accessible, and easy to follow.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty and depth: The core conceptual result (Theorem 1) follows from a direct, three-line algebraic inequality that mirrors standard omnipredictor arguments (e.g., Gopalan et al., 2022a; Hu et al., 2023). Furthermore, the convergence and sample complexity analysis in Theorem 2 is a direct adaptation of existing boosting arguments from the multicalibration literature (Hébert-Johnson et al., 2018; Gopalan et al., 2022b), offering limited new technical insights.

Misleading claim regarding test-time execution: The authors argue on page 3 that their approach is advantageous because 'in the "test phase" we only need one algorithm' (namely, $c^*$). However, evaluating the post-processed predictor $\hat{\gamma}(x)$ on a new context $x$ requires evaluating all boosting updates $\delta_{t+1}(x) = b_{t+1} w_{t+1}(\hat{\gamma}^t(x))$. When $w_{t+1} \in W_1$, evaluating this weight requires running the corresponding decision rule $c \in \mathcal{C}$ on $\gamma(x)$, and when $w_{t+1} \in W_2$, it requires running $c^*$ on $\hat{\gamma}^t(x)$. Consequently, at test time, one must evaluate up to $T$ combinatorial matching algorithms just to compute the input to $c^*$.

Weak motivation against the natural ERM baseline: The standard baseline of estimating the expected value of each rule $c \in \mathcal{C}$ on an i.i.d. dataset and selecting the empirical best achieves the exact same benchmark guarantee with $\tilde{O}(n^2/\varepsilon^2 \log |\mathcal{C}|)$ samples (since matching sizes are at most $n/2$). In contrast, the proposed method requires $\tilde{O}(n^8/\varepsilon^4 \log |\mathcal{C}|)$ samples, involves significant test-time overhead, and does not provide an improved theoretical guarantee over the best $c \in \mathcal{C}$.

Impractical sample complexity: The worst-case sample bound $\tilde{O}(n^8 / \varepsilon^4 \log |\mathcal{C}|)$ scales very poorly with graph size (e.g., for $n=20$, $n^8 \approx 2.5 \times 10^{10}$), severely limiting the practical relevance of the theoretical bounds.

No empirical evaluation: The paper contains no experiments, neither on synthetic graph distributions nor on real-world datasets, to demonstrate how the boosting procedure behaves in practice, how fast it converges, or whether it provides empirical benefits over simply committing to the best heuristic in $\mathcal{C}$.

Discrepancy in sample reuse vs. independent sampling: Algorithm 1 is written as taking a single fixed dataset $D$ of size $N$ as input and reusing it across all iterations. However, the proof of Theorem 2 bounds the sample complexity by multiplying $T$ by the sample complexity of a single CHECK call, implicitly assuming fresh samples at each iteration to avoid statistical dependencies across boosting rounds.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and timely question at the intersection of multicalibration/omniprediction and combinatorial optimization with machine-learned predictions.

The central motivation—that an imperfect or biased edge-weight predictor can lead standard combinatorial solvers to perform poorly, and that post-processing via calibration can help—is conceptually well-grounded.
weaknesses: Misleading claim regarding test-time efficiency: The manuscript claims that 'in the test phase we only need one algorithm' (page 3) and illustrates this in Figure 1. However, this is inaccurate. Line 12-13 of Algorithm 1 shows that the calibrated predictor $\hat{\gamma}(x)$ is computed recursively via updates involving $w_{t+1}$. Whenever $w_{t+1} \in \mathcal{W}_1$, evaluating $w_{t+1}$ requires running the corresponding matching decision rule $c \in \mathcal{C}$ on $\gamma(x)$. Consequently, evaluating $\hat{\gamma}(x)$ at test time requires running up to $T$ different heuristics from $\mathcal{C}$ in addition to running $c^*$ at the end. In contrast, the natural baseline of empirical validation over $\mathcal{C}$ requires executing only a single decision rule at test time.

Technical inconsistency between definitions and Algorithm 1: The proof of Theorem 1 crucially requires the functions in $\mathcal{W}_1$ to be evaluated on the original predictor $\gamma(x)$ (Equation 4), while functions in $\mathcal{W}_2$ are evaluated on $\hat{\gamma}(x)$ (Equation 5). However, Definition 1, Definition 2, and Algorithm 1 conflate these inputs: Line 12 in Algorithm 1 defines $\delta_{t+1}(\cdot) \leftarrow b_{t+1} \cdot w_{t+1}(\hat{\gamma}^t(\cdot))$, passing $\hat{\gamma}^t$ rather than $\gamma$ to $w_{t+1}$. If $w_{t+1} \in \mathcal{W}_1$ is applied to $\hat{\gamma}^t(x)$, the bound in Equation (4) breaks down.

Limited technical novelty: The core theoretical contribution, Theorem 1, is essentially an immediate three-line consequence of the definition of multicalibration applied to the indicators of chosen edges, closely resembling standard omnipredictor/multicalibration arguments (e.g., Gopalan et al., 2022a; Hu et al., 2023).

Severely suboptimal sample complexity compared to standard baselines: The proposed approach requires $\tilde{O}(n^8 / \epsilon^4 \log |\mathcal{C}|)$ samples (or $\tilde{O}(n^8 / \epsilon^2)$ under optimistic assumptions). As the authors note, simply selecting the empirical best decision rule in $\mathcal{C}$ on a hold-out set achieves the same additive guarantee with only $\tilde{O}(n^2 / \epsilon^2 \log |\mathcal{C}|)$ samples (noting matching weights are bounded by $n/2$). Given the astronomical sample complexity and test-time evaluation overhead, the practical utility of the proposed pipeline is unsubstantiated.

Sample reuse and adaptivity issue in Algorithm 1: Algorithm 1 is presented as taking a fixed dataset $D$ and repeatedly calling CHECK on the same samples across iterations (Line 7). Because $\hat{\gamma}^t$ depends on $D$, standard concentration bounds (Hoeffding's inequality) cannot be applied without either sample splitting (drawing fresh samples at each of the $T$ steps) or uniform convergence over the entire function class across iterations.

Total absence of empirical evaluation: The paper contains no experiments or simulations on synthetic or real-world graphs to demonstrate whether multicalibration is computationally viable or offers any practical benefits over simpler post-processing or validation baselines.

strengths: The paper explores an interesting conceptual bridge between multicalibration (from algorithmic fairness) and combinatorial optimization under predicted edge weights.
The paper is clearly written and easy to read, with an intuitive explanation of why naive plug-in estimation can fail.
The idea of post-processing an imperfect predictor using a potential-based boosting approach to guarantee competitive performance against a class of decision rules is conceptually appealing.
weaknesses: Misleading claim regarding test-time inference: The manuscript repeatedly argues as a primary advantage that 'we only need one algorithm' in the test phase (namely $c^*$, the exact max-weight matching algorithm). However, the multicalibrated predictor $\hat{\gamma}(x)$ is defined recursively via the $T$ boosting steps of Algorithm 1. Evaluating $\hat{\gamma}(x)$ on an unseen context $x$ requires evaluating $w_t$, which requires running the audited candidate algorithms $c \in \mathcal{C}$ as well as intermediate calls to $c^*$ at every step $t$. Consequently, test-time inference requires running up to $T = O(n^4 / \varepsilon^2)$ combinatorial optimization problems, completely defeating the claim of an algorithmically simpler test phase.

Unfavorable comparison to the natural baseline: The natural baseline to compete with a finite class of decision rules $\mathcal{C}$ is standard empirical risk minimization (evaluating each rule in $\mathcal{C}$ on validation samples and selecting the empirical maximizer). This baseline requires only $\tilde{O}(n^2 / \varepsilon^2 \log |\mathcal{C}|)$ samples, requires only a single algorithmic execution at test time, and achieves the exact same additive $\varepsilon$-competitiveness. In contrast, the proposed multicalibration approach requires an impractical $\tilde{O}(n^8 / \varepsilon^4 \log |\mathcal{C}|)$ samples and requires $T$ optimization runs per test query.

Limited technical depth and novelty: Theorem 1 is a direct three-line sandwich inequality following immediately from the definition of multicalibration and the optimality of $c^*$. Algorithm 1 and Theorem 2 are essentially direct transcriptions of the standard multicalibration boosting framework (e.g., Gopalan et al., 2022b; Hébert-Johnson et al., 2018). Furthermore, using multicalibration/omnipredictors for constrained linear optimization was already developed in prior work (such as Hu et al., 2023), which diminishes the novelty of the theoretical contribution.

Sample independence inconsistency in Algorithm 1 vs. Theorem 2: Algorithm 1 accepts a single fixed dataset $D = \{(x^j, y^j)\}_{j=1}^N$ and reuses it across all iterations. However, the proof of Theorem 2 applies Hoeffding's inequality at each iteration $t$ as if $\hat{\gamma}^t$ were independent of the samples, and then multiplies the per-step sample complexity $N$ by the number of iterations $T$. To be statistically valid without uniform convergence arguments over the boosting sequence, fresh samples must be drawn at each iteration.

Complete absence of empirical evaluation: The paper contains no experiments or simulations on synthetic or real matching benchmarks to validate whether the multicalibration approach provides any empirical advantage over standard recalibration or baseline model selection.
